We have mass spec and proton NMR data. Need to deduce SMILES.

Mass spec: m/z 179.0946 (most intense). Likely molecular ion (M+). So molecular weight ~179.0946. Need formula. Use typical atomic masses: C=12.0000, H=1.007825, O=15.994915, N=14.003074. 179.0946 suggests maybe C10H11NO2? Let's calculate: C10=120, H11=11.086, N=14.003, O2=31.99 total = 177.079. Not 179. Maybe C9H9ClO? Cl 34.969, C9=108, H9=9.07, O=15.995 total = 143.06. No.

Maybe C11H11O2? C11=132, H11=11.086, O2=31.99 total = 175.076. Not.

C10H13O3? 120+13.102+47.985=181.087. Slight high.

C9H9NO2? 108+9.07+14.003+31.99=163.06.

Let's compute exact mass for C10H11O3? 120+11.086+47.985=179.071. That's close to 179.0946 difference 0.0236. Maybe includes N? C9H9NO3? 108+9.07+14.003+47.985=179.058. Slight low.

C8H7ClO2? 96+7.055+34.969+31.99=150.0.

Better to use isotopic pattern: m/z 179 (100), 180 (11.4), 181 (1). This pattern suggests presence of one chlorine? Chlorine isotopic pattern: 35Cl 75.8% (M), 37Cl 24.2% (M+2). Ratio ~3:1. Here M+1 is 11% not 24% and M+2 is 1% not 24%. So not chlorine. Maybe presence of one bromine? 79Br 50.7% M, 81Br 49.3% M+2 ~1:1. Not.

Pattern suggests maybe one carbon-13 isotopic (M+1) ~1.1% per carbon. For 10 carbons, M+1 ~11% which matches 11.4% at M+1. Good. So 10 carbons. M+2 ~0.1% per two 13C? Actually M+2 from 2 13C ~0.5%? Observed 1% at M+2. So likely 10 carbons.

Thus formula likely C10H?O?N? Let's compute exact mass for C10H?O? etc.

We have M = 179.0946. Subtract 10*12 = 120 => remainder 59.0946. Need to allocate H, O, N.

Let x = number of H (1.007825 each), y = O (15.994915), z = N (14.003074). So 1.007825x + 15.994915y + 14.003074z = 59.0946.

Try y=2, z=0: 2*15.9949=31.9898, remainder 27.1048 => x = 27.1048/1.007825 = 26.88 ~27 H. Too many.

y=3: 47.9847 remainder 11.1099 => x=11.01 ~11 H. So C10H11O3 gives mass: compute exact: C10 120, H11 11.086075, O3 47.984745 = 179.07082. Slight low (by 0.0238). Maybe include N: y=2, z=1: O2 31.9898 + N 14.0031 =45.9929 remainder 13.1017 => H =13.01 ~13 H. So C10H13NO2 mass: 120 + 13.1017 +45.9929 =179.0946 exactly? Let's compute precisely: H13 mass = 13*1.007825 = 13.101725. O2 = 2*15.994915 =31.98983. N =14.003074. Sum =120 +13.101725+31.98983+14.003074 =179.094629. That's exactly the observed 179.09462866255998. Great! So formula C10H13NO2.

Now NMR: 1H NMR signals: 2.58 (t, J=7.4 Hz, 2H), 2.84 (t, J=7.4 Hz, 2H), 3.81 (s, 3H), aromatic region: 7.17 (ddd, 2H), 7.93 (ddd, 2H). So aromatic 4 protons, likely para-disubstituted benzene (AA'BB') giving two doublets, but here ddd each 2H maybe due to ortho coupling? But pattern suggests 4 aromatic protons, likely a para-substituted phenyl ring.

We have a methoxy group (3H singlet at 3.81) typical for OCH3 attached to aromatic (anisole). So anisole ring with para substituent? The aromatic protons would be two sets of 2H each (AA'BB') giving doublets. Here they are ddd but okay.

We also have two aliphatic CH2 groups each 2H as triplets at 2.58 and 2.84 with J=7.4, indicating -CH2-CH2- chain. Likely attached to carbonyl? Possibly an amide: CH2-CH2-CO-? The chemical shift of CH2 adjacent to carbonyl (alpha to carbonyl) is around 2.3-2.5. The other CH2 adjacent to N maybe 2.8. So maybe N-CH2-CH2-CO-OCH3? Wait we have OCH3 (methoxy) maybe as methyl ester. So structure could be methyl 4-aminobutyrate? But aromatic present.

Consider p-anisoyl ethyl amide? Let's think: C10H13NO2 includes aromatic ring (C6H4) plus OCH3 (CH3O) adds C1H3O1. So remaining atoms: C10-6-1 =3 carbons left, H13-4-3 =6 H left, N1 O2-1 =1 O left. So we have a three-carbon chain with N and carbonyl O (amide) maybe: -CO-NH-CH2-CH2-? But we have no NH proton observed (maybe exchangeable not seen). The chain could be -CO-CH2-CH2-N(CH3)? But we have OCH3 already.

Let's assign: aromatic ring (C6H4) para-substituted with OCH3 (methoxy) and CO-CH2-CH2-? Actually OCH3 attached to aromatic as anisole (para-methoxy). The other para substituent could be -CH2-CH2-CO-NH2? But formula includes only one N and one O left (since we used O in methoxy). Wait we have O2 total. One O is in methoxy (as O-CH3). The other O is carbonyl (C=O). So we have an amide carbonyl attached to aromatic? That would be anisamide (p-anisamide) which is p-methoxybenzamide: OCH3 on para, carbonyl attached directly to ring (C=O-NH2). That would have formula C8? Let's compute p-anisamide: C8? Actually anisamide: C8? Let's compute: C8? Wait anisamide is C8? Let's compute: C8? Actually anisamide (p-methoxybenzamide) formula C8? Let's do: aromatic C6H4, OCH3 adds C1H3O1, carbonyl C=O adds C1O1, amide NH2 adds N1H2. Total C8? 6+1+1=8? That's C8? Actually 6+1+1 =8 carbons. But we need C10. So not.

Our formula C10H13NO2 suggests aromatic C6H4 plus OCH3 (C1H3O) plus carbonyl C1O plus side chain C2H? plus N? Let's compute: aromatic C6H4, OCH3 adds C1H3O1, carbonyl C1O1, side chain C2H? plus N1? Let's sum: Carbons:6+1+1+2=10 good. O atoms: OCH3 O1, carbonyl O1 =2 good. N1 present. Hydrogens: aromatic H4, OCH3 H3, side chain CH2-CH2 gives H4, plus maybe NH? That would be H? total H =4+3+4+? =11 plus maybe NH? But we need H13. So we need extra 2 H, maybe NH2? Actually amide N may have H2 (NH2) adding 2 H. That would give total H13. So structure: p-methoxy phenyl attached to carbonyl (C=O) attached to NH2? That's p-anisamide (p-methoxybenzamide) which we earlier thought had C8? Let's recalc: p-anisamide formula: C8? Wait p-anisamide: C6H4 (ring) + OCH3 (CH3O) = C1H3O1, carbonyl C=O = C1O1, amide NH2 = N1H2. Total C =6+1+1=8? That's 8 carbons, but we need 10. Something off: Actually the carbonyl carbon is part of the aromatic substituent? In benzamide, the carbonyl carbon is attached directly to the ring, not extra carbon beyond the ring. So the carbonyl carbon is counted as part of the substituent but not extra beyond the aromatic carbon count? The aromatic ring already includes the carbon bearing the carbonyl. So the carbonyl carbon is part of the ring? In benzamide, the formula is C7H7NO? Wait benzamide formula is C7H7NO? Let's check: benzamide C7H7NO? Actually benzamide: C6H5CONH2 => C7H7NO? plus O? So C7H7NO? plus O? Actually C6H5 (C6H5) + C=O (C1O1) + NH2 (N1H2) => C7H7NO? plus O? So C7H7NO? Wait O count: carbonyl O1, plus maybe? So C7H7NO? Actually formula C7H7NO? Let's compute: C7 H7 N1 O1? That's C7H7NO? But known benzamide formula is C7H7NO? Let's quickly recall: benzamide C7H7NO? Actually I think benzamide is C7H7NO? plus O? I'm confused.

Let's compute: C6H5 (C6 H5) + C (carbonyl) = C7, H? carbonyl carbon has no H. So total H5. Add NH2 adds 2 H => H7. O1 from carbonyl. So C7H7NO? That's C7H7NO? plus O? Wait we have O1. So formula C7H7NO? Actually need O1. So C7H7NO? That's missing O. Should be C7H7NO? maybe O1 is included. So C7H7NO? Actually typical formula for benzamide is C7H7NO? Let's quickly check memory: benzamide formula is C7H7NO? I think it's C7H7NO? plus O? Actually I recall benzamide is C7H7NO? maybe C7H7NO? I'm not sure.

Anyway, p-anisamide would be C8H9NO2? Let's compute: add OCH3 adds C1H3O1. So C8H? H5+3+2 =10? Wait H5 from ring, plus 3 from OCH3 =8, plus 2 from NH2 =10. So C8H10? Actually need to recalc: ring H4 (since para substitution reduces H count to 4). So C6H4. Add OCH3 (C1H3O1). Add carbonyl C1O1. Add NH2 (N1H2). Total C =8, H =4+3+2=9, N1, O2. So C8H9NO2. That's not our formula.

Our formula C10H13NO2 has two extra carbons and four extra hydrogens compared to C8H9NO2. So maybe the carbonyl is part of an ester (COOCH3) rather than amide? But we have N present. Could be methyl 4-(2-oxoethyl)aniline? Let's think: aromatic ring with methoxy (OCH3) and side chain -CH2-CH2-CO-NH2? That would add C3 (CH2-CH2-CO) plus N and O? But carbonyl O already counted, plus maybe extra O? Actually carbonyl O is one O, we need total O2, one is methoxy O, other is carbonyl O. So side chain -CH2-CH2-CO- attached to aromatic (as acyl side chain). Then N is part of amide? Wait carbonyl attached to N? If carbonyl is part of amide, O is carbonyl O, N attached to carbonyl. The side chain would be -CO-NH2 attached to aromatic? That's benzamide again. Not.

Alternative: aromatic ring with methoxy and side chain -CH2-CH2-COOCH3 (ester). That would have OCH3 as part of ester, but we already have OCH3 attached to aromatic? Actually OCH3 could be part of ester attached to aromatic carbonyl (anisic acid methyl ester). That would be methyl p-methoxybenzoate (methyl anisate). Formula: C9? Let's compute: aromatic C6H4, OCH3 attached to carbonyl (ester) adds C1H3O1, carbonyl C1O1, plus methoxy on ring adds C1H3O1? Wait anisate has methoxy on ring and methyl ester. So total C =6+1+1+1 =9? Actually ring C6, carbonyl carbon C1, methoxy on ring C1, methyl of ester C1 => total C9. That's C9? But we need C10. So maybe both OCH3 groups are present: one as methoxy on ring, one as methyl ester. That's C9? Let's compute: C6 (ring) + carbonyl C1 =7, plus OCH3 on ring C1 =8, plus OCH3 of ester C1 =9. So C9. Not enough.

Our formula C10 suggests side chain of two carbons beyond carbonyl (like -CO-CH2-CH3). But we have N present, so maybe it's an amide with ethyl group on nitrogen: -CO-NH-CH2-CH3? That would add C2H5 plus N and O. Let's test: aromatic ring C6H4, methoxy on ring C1H3O1, carbonyl C1O1, N attached to ethyl C2H5. Total C =6+1+1+2=10 good. Hydrogens: ring H4, methoxy H3, ethyl H5 =12, plus maybe NH? The N may have H (NH) giving 1 more =13. So formula C10H13NO2 matches! Good.

Thus structure: p-methoxy phenyl attached to carbonyl (amide) attached to ethylamine (N-ethyl). So N-ethyl p-anisamide (N-ethyl-4-methoxybenzamide). That would have aromatic 4H, methoxy singlet 3H, ethyl group: CH2 (adjacent to N) appears as triplet? Actually N-CH2-CH3: N-CH2 (CH2 attached to N) appears as quartet? Wait coupling to CH3 gives quartet (J~7). CH3 appears as triplet. But observed: two triplets at 2.58 and 2.84 each 2H. That's not ethyl pattern. Ethyl would be 2H quartet and 3H triplet. Here both are 2H triplets, indicating -CH2-CH2- chain where each CH2 couples to the other (triplet). So N-CH2-CH2-CO? That is N-CH2-CH2-CO attached to aromatic? That would be N-ethyl attached to carbonyl? Actually N-CH2-CH2-CO-? Wait carbonyl attached to aromatic, N attached to CH2-CH2? That would be N-(2-phenyl)?? Let's propose: p-methoxybenzoyl attached to N-CH2-CH2-? The N is attached to CH2-CH2-? The N may be part of a secondary amide: -CO-N-CH2-CH2-? The other side of N is maybe hydrogen (NH). But we have two CH2 groups both triplets, consistent with -CO-N-CH2-CH2-? The CH2 adjacent to carbonyl (alpha to carbonyl) would be on the carbonyl side, not N side. Wait chain: aromatic-CO-N-CH2-CH2-? The carbonyl carbon attached to aromatic, then N attached to CH2-CH2-? The CH2 next to N (beta to carbonyl) appears at ~2.8 (adjacent to N). The CH2 next to carbonyl (alpha) appears at ~2.5 (adjacent to carbonyl). Both are triplets due to coupling to each other. That matches observed chemical shifts: 2.58 (t) likely alpha to carbonyl, 2.84 (t) beta to N. Good.

Thus structure: N-ethyl-4-methoxybenzamide? Wait N-ethyl would be -CO-N-CH2CH3, not CH2CH2. So not.

Our chain is -CO-N-CH2-CH2-? The terminal group maybe H (NH-CH2-CH2-CO-Ph). That's N-(2-oxoethyl)?? Actually that's 2-phenoxy? Let's think: The amide nitrogen attached to CH2-CH2-? The other side of CH2-CH2 maybe hydrogen (i.e., N-CH2-CH2-? but no further substituent). That would be N-(2-oxoethyl)?? Not.

But we have only one carbonyl O, so the chain ends at N. So the molecule is 4-methoxyphenylacetamide? Wait phenylacetamide would be -CO-CH2-NH2. That would have CH2 (2H) adjacent to carbonyl, and NH2 (exchangeable). Not two CH2.

Our observed two CH2 suggests -CO-CH2-CH2-NH-? Actually carbonyl attached to CH2 (alpha) then CH2 then NH? That would be a propanamide: phenyl-CO-CH2-CH2-NH2 (3-phenylpropionamide). But the N is at terminal, not attached to carbonyl. However the carbonyl is attached to aromatic? Wait phenyl-CO-CH2-CH2-NH2 would be phenylpropionamide (phenyl attached to carbonyl). That would have aromatic 5 H (if unsubstituted). But we have para substitution with methoxy, so 4 H. Good. The chain: carbonyl attached directly to aromatic (as benzoyl). Then CH2-CH2-NH2. That matches two CH2 triplets. The NH2 may be exchangeable not seen. So formula: aromatic C6H4, methoxy C1H3O, carbonyl C1O, chain C2H4, NH2 N1H2. Total C =6+1+1+2=10, H =4+3+4+2=13, O2, N1. Perfect! So structure is 4-methoxyphenylpropionamide (p-anisic acid propanamide) also called 4-methoxyphenylpropionamide.

SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)CCN

Check: aromatic ring with methoxy at para: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)CCN. That has N attached to CH2 (terminal). Yes.

Let's validate with tool.
